title: Futures
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/0/body: A **futures contract** is an agreement to buy or sell an asset in the **future** at a price set **today**. When you trade futures, you don't buy the asset itself; you just take a contract on **its price change**.
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/1/body: Traditional futures have an **expiry date**. A **perpetual contract**, common on crypto exchanges, never expires, so you can hold it as long as you like. A mechanism called the **funding rate** keeps its price close to the spot price.
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/2/prompt: What's the main difference between a perpetual contract and traditional futures?
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/2/options/2: Perpetuals have no leverage at all
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/2/options/3: With perpetuals, you receive the actual coin
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/2/explanati: Perpetual means "forever": it never expires, and it stays close to the spot price through the funding rate instead.
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/3/statement: When you go long Bitcoin on futures, you own real bitcoin and can move it to your wallet.
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/3/explanati: On futures, you only hold a contract on the price, not the coin itself. For real ownership, you have to buy on the spot market.
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/4/body: To open a position, you only put up part of its value as **margin (collateral)**: **margin = position value ÷ leverage**. At 10x leverage, margin is one tenth of the position value, but profit and loss are calculated on the **full position value**.
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/4/tip: Exchanges usually calculate liquidation with the mark price: a reference price built from the prices on several exchanges.
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/5/prompt: You want to open a 3,000 USDT position at 5x leverage. How much margin do you need?
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/6/sentence: A ___ contract has no expiry, and the ___ keeps its price close to spot.
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/6/explanati: Since a perpetual never expires, the funding rate acts like a rubber band, pulling its price back toward spot.
lessons/leverage-u1-l1/steps/7/pairs/0/m: A contract on a future price
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/0/body: **Long** means you profit when price rises, and **short** means you profit when price falls. On futures, going short is as easy as going long, and you don't need to own the coin first.
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/1/title: How are profit and loss calculated?
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/1/body: **Profit or loss = position size × price change.** Leverage doesn't change this number; it just takes less margin from you. That's why profit and loss get multiplied **relative to your margin**.
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/2/prompt: You went short at the "Entry" line. How is your position doing right now?
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/2/options/0: In a loss; price is above your short entry
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/2/options/1: In profit, because price went up
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/2/options/2: Break-even; funding makes up for it
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/2/explanati: A short profits when price falls below the entry. Here, price has climbed about $1,450 above your entry, so you're in a loss.
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/3/prompt: You shorted 0.5 ETH at 3,000 USDT, and price has reached 2,800. What's your profit or loss?
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/3/explanati: Price fell 200 USDT, and a short profits from a drop: 0.5 × 200 = 100 USDT profit.
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/4/body: At 10x leverage, every **1%** price move means about a **10%** change in your margin, in both directions. At 50x, that same 1% is **50% of your margin**. That's why high leverage leaves very little room before **liquidation**.
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/4/tip: Think of leverage as a way to put up less margin, not a way to make bigger profits.
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/5/statement: If you go long at 20x and price drops 2%, you've lost about 40% of your margin.
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/5/explanati: 20 × 2% = 40%. At 20x, every 1% move against you wipes out about 20% of your margin.
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/6/prompt: On futures, you can go short too. Given this structure and the last candle, which side makes more sense?
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/6/explanati: The trend is down (lower highs and lower lows), price has reached old broken support that's now resistance, and the last candle got rejected with a long upper wick. More downside is likely, but not guaranteed; you need a stop loss above the last candle's high.
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/7/sentence: If you think price will fall, you go ___, and if price rises, your position takes a ___.
lessons/leverage-u1-l2/steps/7/explanati: A short profits from a drop, so a rising price means a loss for a short.
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/0/body: Since perpetuals never expire, exchanges keep their price close to spot with the **funding rate**. Funding is a **periodic payment between longs and shorts**, made **every 8 hours** on many exchanges.
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/1/body: When funding is **positive**, **longs pay shorts**; this usually happens when the perpetual trades above spot and demand for longs is higher. When it's **negative**, **shorts pay longs**.
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/1/tip: Very positive funding means lots of leveraged longs are in the market. Many traders see that as a sign one side is getting crowded.
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/2/statement: When the funding rate is positive, shorts pay longs.
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/2/explanati: It's the other way around: positive funding means longs pay shorts. That makes going long more expensive and pulls the perpetual's price back toward spot.
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/3/body: Funding is calculated on the **full position value**, not your margin, so with high leverage, the cost is bigger relative to your margin. You usually only pay or receive funding if your position is open **at the funding time**.
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/4/prompt: You hold a long worth 20,000 USDT, and funding is +0.05%. What happens each funding period?
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/4/explanati: 20,000 × 0.05% = 10 USDT. Funding is positive and you're long, so you're the one paying.
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/5/prompt: With 500 USDT margin at 20x, you hold a 10,000 USDT long. Funding is +0.05% every 8 hours. What percent of your margin is the daily funding cost?
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/5/explanati: 10,000 × 0.05% = 5 USDT per period; 3 periods a day = 15 USDT; 15 ÷ 500 = 3% of your margin per day. Over 10 days, about 30% of your margin goes to funding alone.
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/6/statement: The funding rate usually passes between traders themselves; the exchange doesn't keep it as a fee.
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/6/explanati: On big exchanges, funding is taken from one side (say, the longs) and paid to the other. Trading fees are a separate cost.
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/7/prompt: You plan to hold a leveraged long for a few weeks, and funding stays high and positive. What matters most here?
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/7/options/0: Over time, funding eats a big chunk of your profit
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/7/options/2: Funding is only paid on the first day
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/7/options/3: Higher leverage makes funding cost zero
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/7/explanati: Funding repeats every period and is charged on the full position value. For long holds, you need to build this cost into your profit target.
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/8/sentence: On many exchanges, funding is paid every ___ hours and calculated on the full ___ value.
lessons/leverage-u1-l3/steps/8/explanati: An 8-hour period is common on many exchanges (some use a different period for certain contracts). The basis is the position value, not the margin.
